title: Expert blames climate change for Nepal flash floods | NHK WORLD-JAPAN News - nhk.or.jp
description: Expert blames climate change for Nepal flash floods | NHK WORLD-JAPAN News  nhk.or.jp
publisher.title: nhk.or.jp
full_article:
A Nepalese expert on glaciers says climate change played a significant role in the massive flash floods that devastated border areas between Nepal and China.

Sudan Bikash Maharjan is a researcher at the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development, based in Kathmandu. He spoke to NHK on Thursday about his analysis of topographical data and satellite images to identify the cause of the flash floods.

Maharjan said the studies suggest the possibility that a glacier at an altitude of about 5,100 meters had melted, exposing part of the rock surface of the slope, and that melted water had permeated into the rock through cracks, making the slope unstable.

He said the analysis shows when the glacier and huge rock mass collapsed, the debris fell about 1,000 meters and crashed into another glacier at the bottom of the valley. He said the frictional energy and force of the collision melted and pulverized the valley glacier, resulting in water and debris gushing down the valley.

Maharjan said climate change played a significant role in the occurrence of the deadly flooding. He pointed out that the glacier area across Nepal has decreased by 32 percent just over a 40-year period. He said climate change, especially rising temperatures, has caused a substantial loss in glacier area by accelerating the pace of melting.

He also warned that changes in the landscape of the valley due to the disaster could significantly increase the risk of landslides and flooding in the future.

He said systems to issue alarms and monitor conditions in the mountain regions should be strengthened to prepare for future calamities.

title: Dams or death traps? How Nepal’s deadly floods expose fragility of Himalayan energy - NPR
description: Dams or death traps? How Nepal’s deadly floods expose fragility of Himalayan energy  NPR
publisher.title: NPR
full_article:
Transcript

SCOTT SIMON, HOST:

A month since a glacier and its bedrock collapsed into a river valley in the Himalayas, triggering flash floods. More than 7,500 people have died or cannot be found. And that includes workers who were trapped in a dozen hydropower plants built alongside the stretch of a river in Nepal - plants that are now buried. One tunneling expert, Arnold Dix, described it like this.

ARNOLD DIX: Like a bomb's gone off, it's removed the power stations from the surface like they're just not there.

SIMON: And as NPR's Diaa Hadid reports, that's triggered scrutiny over how these projects are being built in the Himalayas.

DIAA HADID, BYLINE: Rescuers haven't found any survivors in one of the biggest hydropower plants that was buried under the mud. The Nepali army estimates there were 50 people there. It's called the Upper Trishuli-1 and cost over half $1 billion. It was backed with hundreds of millions of dollars in loans led by the World Bank. It was under construction. Now it's under the mud. These buried hydropower plants were built along the stretch of a steep river valley called the Trishuli.

AUSTIN LORD: This, in particular, is a really high-risk area to build dams. But nonetheless, the industry started there, and it gained momentum.

HADID: Austin Lord works on disaster risk reduction in the Himalayan region at the Stimson Center. Lord says the area is particularly vulnerable to glacial lakes bursting, and this was the third year in a row there had been deadly floods. But he says the momentum to build here began more than a decade ago because there were roads and proximity to the border with Chinese-administered Tibet, so supplies could easily come in.

LORD: It's an obvious choice for a hydropower developer or someone looking through that lens.

HADID: But Lord and others argue that developers long diminish the chance of one-off events, which allowed them to greenlight projects that perhaps should not have proceeded at that scale or design.

LORD: I've called it strategic ignorance.

HADID: Experts also told NPR that developers typically did not account for the risk of building so many projects in the same area, which is why critics like Parineeta Dandekar accuse the World Bank of crafting a myopic risk assessment that allowed it to go ahead with the Upper Trishuli-1 project. She says it ignored the danger from the constant blasting and dynamiting of mountains to build these projects, including to carve out tunnels.

PARINEETA DANDEKAR: Imagine the amount of stressors at play when it's 12 times across a single steep river basin in Himalayas.

HADID: The World Bank said in a statement that preventative measures were taken against floods, landslides and other events. The bank said it reflected evidence when the assessment was made in 2018. And experts do disagree on whether the constant building had an impact on the events of August 26 that led to devastating flash flooding. Dipak Gyawali is a hydropower engineer with the Nepal Academy of Science and Technology.

DIPAK GYAWALI: Dynamiting is almost nothing. It's like scratching on top of a skin. That's all.

HADID: Dynamiting in the Himalayas is like scratching your skin. Two scientific assessments suggest a different man-made problem was at play that triggered the flash floods in August. Global warming exacerbated the melting of a glacier in its bedrock. They snapped off in August, falling into the river valley, triggering flash floods. And it's unclear if any major backer took the rapidly changing climate into account for the Upper Trishuli-1 Project.

One major funder was the Asian Development Bank. In 2024, they dispatched independent experts who visited the site, and they reported that no climate resilience assessment was undertaken. The independent experts described that as a significant gap. The Asian Development Bank hasn't responded to NPR's question as to whether that assessment was ultimately undertaken. Dandekar, who is critical of this hydropower project, says the World Bank and other backers need to ask...

DANDEKAR: Are they safe for the ecosystems and communities and the workers, or are we just putting them in danger over and over again? Where does the accountability lie?

HADID: Accountability for the dozens of workers who are now entombed in these hydropower plants. Advocates say they hope this devastating flood might prompt a rethink of how hydropower is constructed across the Himalayas. They're particularly worried about a massive hydropower plant and dam that China began building in Tibet last year. It's estimated it will provide power to 300 million people. Chinese authorities say the hydro project is safe. But in July, Chinese geologists reported that the dam was being constructed over an active fault line, risking the integrity of the project's infrastructure.

SHYAM SARAN: If something happens there, it is going to be a monumental disaster.

HADID: That's retired Indian Ambassador Shyam Saran, who served as the prime minister's special envoy for climate change. The Chinese project is being built near the border with India. One accident, he says, could wipe away downstream communities in his country. But even as India worries about the impact, it's building its own massive hydropower plant and dam just downstream.

Diaa Hadid, NPR News, Mumbai.

title: Shah returns from UNGA after putting climate crisis at centre of Nepal’s global pitch - The Kathmandu Post
description: Shah returns from UNGA after putting climate crisis at centre of Nepal’s global pitch  The Kathmandu Post
publisher.title: The Kathmandu Post
full_article:
Prime Minister Balendra Shah returned home on Saturday after participating in the high-level week of the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly in New York, where he put Nepal’s climate vulnerability, climate justice and the need for stronger international support at the centre of his address.

He was welcomed at Tribhuvan International Airport by Acting Prime Minister and Finance Minister Swarnim Wagle and other ministers. No official ceremony was held at the airport’s VVIP lounge upon his arrival from New York.

Shah had left Kathmandu for New York on September 22 to attend the high-level week, which is being held at the UN headquarters from September 22 to 28. The theme of this year’s General Assembly is “Restoring Trust, Managing Transformation: A United Nations that Delivers for All.”

Addressing the General Debate on September 24, Shah presented the recent devastating Bhotekoshi floods as a serious impact of the climate crisis and a warning to the world. He drew the international community’s attention to the heavy loss of life and property caused by the disaster, as well as its impact on physical infrastructure and livelihoods.

He said Nepal is at the forefront of the climate crisis and, despite contributing less than 0.1 percent of global greenhouse gas emissions, is suffering disproportionate and severe impacts from climate change. Climate change, he said, is not merely a humanitarian issue for Nepal but also a development emergency.

Shah also highlighted the impact of climate change on Himalayan ecology, saying that melting glaciers and permafrost are increasing the risks of ice-rock avalanches, floods and landslides.

He proposed establishing a Himalayan Climate Resilience Mechanism to monitor vulnerable glacial lakes, strengthen early warning systems and facilitate cross-border coordination during disasters.

He said climate change should not be turned into a subject of geopolitical conflict and stressed that solutions should be sought on the basis of shared responsibility and solidarity, in accordance with the principle of Common but Differentiated Responsibilities and Respective Capabilities.

Shah said countries that have historically played a greater role in causing the climate crisis and have greater resources and capabilities should shoulder greater responsibility for addressing it. He called on the international community to put climate justice into practice.

He also stressed the need for grant-based international assistance for rehabilitation and reconstruction following climate-induced disasters. Existing climate finance mechanisms, including the Loss and Damage Fund, he said, should make the mobilisation of resources simpler and easier.

Highlighting Nepal’s contribution to environmental protection through forest conservation, hydropower development, the promotion of electric vehicles and climate adaptation efforts at the local level, Shah called for greater investment in climate resilience, stronger infrastructure, effective early warning systems and innovative technologies.

He called for an end to relying solely on ad hoc responses to climate-induced disasters and stressed the need to develop a culture of preparedness.

Climate justice, he said, should not be limited to financial assistance but should also ensure distributive and procedural justice.

Reaffirming Nepal’s unwavering faith in multilateralism, Shah said Nepal has confidence in the United Nations to build a system that listens to the voices of small and poor countries and delivers just outcomes.

During his visit, Shah held a meeting with UN Secretary-General António Guterres.

Guterres expressed deep condolences over the loss of life and property in the Bhotekoshi disaster and said the United Nations stands in solidarity with Nepal on climate issues.

Shah thanked Guterres for his goodwill towards Nepal and congratulated him on his successful tenure. Referring to the heavy losses suffered by Nepal in the Bhotekoshi disaster, Shah said the risk of glacial lake outburst floods remains high.

The two also discussed the rehabilitation of people living along riverbanks and green reconstruction. They also discussed support for extending the timeline for Nepal’s graduation from the list of Least Developed Countries (LDCs).

Shah also held a meeting with Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, during which the two sides discussed various issues of bilateral interest.

Khanal holds meetings on UNGA sidelines

Foreign Minister Shishir Khanal has been participating in ministerial-level meetings of the Least Developed Countries, Landlocked Developing Countries, Non-Aligned Movement, and G77 and China, among others, held during the General Assembly.

Khanal has also been addressing other high-level discussions and side events organised by the United Nations.

He has been holding meetings with counterparts from various friendly countries, including Nepal’s neighbours, as well as high-level UN officials.

title: Can Nepal’s Young Turks learn to govern? - Nepali Times
description: Can Nepal’s Young Turks learn to govern?  Nepali Times
publisher.title: Nepali Times
full_article:
Something keeps coming back to me as I watch from afar Nepal’s new Young Turks in government.

Whatever the slips here and there — and whether open competition makes sense as a blanket mechanism for appointments like ambassadors — something rather consequential is being attempted.

Nepal’s political parties and government have long operated mostly through a ‘relational system’: who knows whom, who belongs to whose network, who owes whom. It is one of the ways the extractive politics of the past 30 years, and for many decades prior to that, worked.

The repeated push toward open competition for vice chancellorships and many other positions are almost an act of constructive destruction — an attempt to dismantle that relational system, popularly known as the politics of भागबन्डा, and gradually replace it with a more impersonal governing system, where rules and procedures matter more than personal access.

Ambassadorial appointments provide the latest experiment. More than 4,400 people applied after the government opened the positions to public applications, with 13 nominees emerging from the first round of selections.

Open competition is not magic. Nor am I convinced it is the right mechanism for every appointment. I offer a mixed hybrid method in my Nepal Unplugged essay.

Essentially, diplomacy requires judgment, experience, political understanding and interpersonal skills that cannot easily be captured by an application form. An open advertisement can also lead to a closed selection process if what happens afterward is less transparent.

But that is almost secondary. These young leaders may not always get the mechanism right. They are young, educated and energetic, but relatively inexperienced in the unforgiving business of governing.

Still, they deserve credit for daring to take on something much deeper than individual appointments: a governing habit built over generations. That may ultimately be more consequential than who wins any particular vacancy.

But daring to dismantle an old system and learning how to govern are two different things. They have done the first, but the latter is yet to be seen.

The recent 3% levies on private education and health offer an interesting example. The education levy and argued that its underlying equity principle was defensible, even if the instrument was problematic. The government introduced it, encountered strong public resistance, and quickly withdrew it.

Was that immaturity or responsiveness? A young government should be able to experiment, discover that an instrument is not working as intended, and change course. More worrying would be a government so invested in appearing decisive that it loses the capacity to learn. I am a big fan of learning by doing.

But that does not mean learning only after making avoidable mistakes. Experimentation is valuable if it gradually produces better consultation, better sequencing, better anticipation of unintended consequences — and fewer avoidable mistakes the next time around.

The qualities that help disrupt an old political equilibrium are not necessarily the same qualities needed to construct the next one. Breaking an entrenched system requires courage, impatience and a willingness to challenge convention. They did that. Or, more accurately, the youths who came on the streets on 8 September 2025 demanding this change forced that disruption.

Governing requires some rather less exciting virtues: institutional memory, administrative competence, consultation and occasionally slowing down enough to think. That includes sitting and planning and not rushing to enter the tunnels even though the intentions may be right.

And the clock may be running faster than they realise. The next thing they should understand is that public memory is thin.

We hardly need to travel very far for evidence. Since the restoration of multiparty democracy in 1990, Nepal has repeatedly experienced waves of extraordinary political hope followed by disappointment, and another search for change. The 1990 movement, the upheavals surrounding 2006, and most recently the Gen Z uprising all remind us how quickly apparently settled political equilibria can break or simply collapse.

History offers an even more dramatic reminder. In August 1792, the people of Paris rose against the old order and helped bring into being the National Convention. Less than three years later, an angry crowd invaded that very Convention demanding bread and political change.

Nepal is obviously not revolutionary France. But these lessons travel rather well: people who help create a new political order do not remain in a grateful mood forever.

The same citizens who gave these young leaders an extraordinary mandate will not spend the next five years congratulating them for defeating the old parties. At some point — and probably sooner than they expect — the reference point will change.

People will ask much simpler questions. Are schools better? Are hospitals functioning? Are jobs appearing? Is corruption declining? Does the bureaucracy work better?

This is also where Nepal’s media has an unusually important role to play. Neither cheerleading nor reflexive cynicism will help much. Perhaps what we need is optimism with skepticism.

When the government challenges an entrenched patronage network, give it credit. When an open process becomes shady, ask questions. When it makes a mistake, say so. When it corrects one, acknowledge that too. A young government needs room to learn. It does not need a free pass.

There may also be a quieter consequence worth watching. If these experiments begin changing what citizens expect from government, the effects will not stop with those currently in power. The older parties will face pressures of their own to self-reflect, reform and compete under those changing expectations.

That could ultimately be one of the more consequential effects of this political disruption: not simply replacing one set of political actors with another, but changing the standards against which all of them must compete.

The Young Turks have already disturbed a political equilibrium that many Nepalis had come to regard as almost immovable. But constructive destruction has two words: disrupting the old relational system may turn out to be the easier part, and constructing an impersonal system of rules, competence and accountability will be much harder.

In the end, politics promises no certainty at the ballot box. But leaving behind a legacy of norm entrepreneurship — raising the bar for how governance is conducted, even for those who come after them — might just be the most consequential outcome of all.

Read also: Win-win-win, Alok K Bohara

title: Month after deadly Nepal floods, thousands still missing - National Herald
description: Month after deadly Nepal floods, thousands still missing  National Herald
publisher.title: National Herald
full_article:
A month after devastating flash floods struck Nepal’s northern and central districts, the human and infrastructural toll remains staggering as authorities struggle to account for survivors and victims. According to the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA), 1,453 bodies have been recovered so far, but nearly 5,300 people remain missing.

The floodwaters originated near the Nepal-Tibet border on August 26, triggered by flash floods that swept downstream along the Bhotekoshi River. This disaster destroyed homes, vehicles, roads, bridges, and hydropower projects, isolating many communities. Alongside Nepal's losses, 43 fatalities were reported in Tibet, where over 500 people are still unaccounted for.

Of the approximately 13,795 people rescued across affected areas, more than 1,000 remain housed in 21 holding centers, including large numbers in Nuwakot, Rasuwa, and Dhading districts. However, the identification of deceased victims has proven to be a massive challenge. Many bodies were severely damaged or fragmented, with only 112 identified and returned to families to date. The Nepal Police have therefore turned to DNA profiling, collecting 1,329 samples from discovered remains and 2,060 from relatives of missing individuals. Details on 1,421 unidentified bodies have also been published on the police website, aiding families in their search.

Infrastructure damage has been extensive, with around 40 kilometers of roads and 41 motorable bridges wiped out between Rasuwa and Dhading districts. These losses have severed important connections, complicating relief efforts. Temporary tracks and Bailey bridges—some installed by the Nepal Army—have been crucial in restoring connectivity. Nonetheless, limited air transport capacity restricts the timely delivery of relief supplies to remote communities.

Search operations continue at damaged hydropower projects, where workers remain missing. Bodies have been recovered from tunnels at the Chilime and Upper Trishuli-1 sites, but searches persist.

Compounding difficulties, recent heavy rainfall has triggered fresh landslides, blocking roads and disrupting rescue and recovery operations. As Nepal endures this ongoing crisis, authorities and communities remain united in efforts to rescue survivors and rebuild vital infrastructure.

title: Washout seals top spot for Nepal. Sri Lanka wait in quarterfinals - The Kathmandu Post
description: Washout seals top spot for Nepal. Sri Lanka wait in quarterfinals  The Kathmandu Post
publisher.title: The Kathmandu Post
full_article:
Nepal’s final preliminary group match of the 20th Asian Games against hosts Japan was abandoned due to heavy rain on Saturday, but the Rhinos had already done enough to advance as Group A’s topper and book a quarterfinal clash against Sri Lanka .

Put into bat after losing the toss at Korogi Athletic Park in Aichi, Nepal managed 149/4 in a match shortened by rain to 15 overs per side.

However, persistent torrential downpours following the conclusion of Nepal’s innings forced the umpires to call off the fixture. Nepal and Japan then shared points.

Having defeated Afghanistan by five wickets on Friday, Nepal topped Group A to seal their spot in the last eight. Hosts Japan, who had lost to Afghanistan, were eliminated from the competition.

In the quarterfinal stage, group winners Nepal will face seeded heavyweights Sri Lanka for a place in the semifinals. Group A runners-up Afghanistan will take on India in another quarterfinal fixture.

Rain also disrupted Group B action on Saturday, with the second match between Malaysia and Oman abandoned without a single ball being bowled. Group B winners Malaysia advance to face Bangladesh in the quarterfinals, while runners-up Hong Kong take on Pakistan.

Earlier in the day, explosive half-centuries from Sundeep Jora and Lokesh Bam set up Nepal’s formidable total. Jora remained undefeated on a belligerent 57 off 32 balls, while Bam stayed not out at 52 off 22 deliveries. The pair combined for a 65-run partnership off 30 balls for the fifth wicket.

After openers Kushal Bhurtel (4 off 12) and Aasif Sheikh (21 off 15) fell cheaply alongside Kushal Malla (2 off 5) and Gulshan Jha (2 off 6), Jora took charge of the innings with supreme confidence, hammering five fours and three sixes. He reached his half-century when a Japanese fielder dropped a catch at the boundary ropes on 49, resulting in a boundary.

At the other end, Bam, who also got a lifeline, brought up his maiden T20I half-century in thrilling fashion, launching a six off the final ball of the innings. Striking one four and six sixes, Bam brought the crowd of nearly 2,000 Nepali supporters to their feet.

For Japan, Reo Sakurano-Thomas, Ibrahim Takahashi, Jake Kusuda-Nairn and Declan Suzuki picked up a wicket each.

title: For 26 years, India has searched passengers at Kathmandu airport. Nepal can’t say why - The Kathmandu Post
description: For 26 years, India has searched passengers at Kathmandu airport. Nepal can’t say why  The Kathmandu Post
publisher.title: The Kathmandu Post
full_article:
Anyone flying out of Kathmandu’s Tribhuvan International Airport on an Indian-registered aircraft undergoes an additional security screening just before boarding. At a screening point on a raised platform on the airport apron, staffed by Indian security personnel, passengers are frisked, and their luggage is subjected to a thorough hand search. It’s hardly a secret; nor is it new. But after more than a quarter of a century, it is simply part of boarding.

An official at the Civil Aviation Authority of Nepal said Air India and IndiGo both deploy Indian staff at Tribhuvan in three shifts. Of the 12 to 15 people working a single flight, six to eight are Indian employees stationed on the apron. They wear the heavy boots of security personnel. Passengers are directed one at a time into a trolley screened on all four sides, where the Indian staff search their bodies and their hand baggage. Nepali staff assist, but are kept out of the search itself. “Nepali staff are not given a role in the major duty in the apron area for India-bound flights,” the official said, who agreed to provide details about the staffing and search on condition of anonymity.

No Nepali agency can produce any document that originally authorized this. Over several weeks, Kantipur asked officials at the Ministry of Culture, Tourism and Civil Aviation, the Civil Aviation Authority of Nepal, and the Ministry of Home Affairs if they could locate the relevant records. Each time they referred the question to one of the other agencies.

What does exist is on the Indian side. When Indian Airlines resumed its flights to Kathmandu, after a five-month suspension following a hijacking episode, Indian news agencies reported that Nepal had accepted the airline’s demand for an additional X-ray machine and a final check by Indian security personnel at the airport, on top of Nepal’s own screening.

Weeks later, India’s minister of state for external affairs at the time, Ajit Panja, told the lower house, the Lok Sabha , that additional measures required by the airlines had been put in place, that Indian experts had assessed the steps taken by Nepal’s Civil Aviation Authority and were satisfied, and that the security arrangements would be reviewed on an ongoing basis. He did not say who would be conducting the security checks.

Nepal has never publicly acknowledged those terms, or said whether it agreed to anything in writing.

Questions about Nepal’s sovereignty have surfaced from time to time, but none of the successive governments have sought to review the arrangement. India, meanwhile, has repeatedly pressed for more — including permission to place sky marshals on its flights out of Kathmandu. Nepali officials have turned down the demand or quietly shelved it each time.

***

On December 24, 1999, Indian Airlines Flight IC814 took off from Kathmandu. Minutes later, the aircraft, carrying 190 people, was hijacked by five men later identified by Indian investigators as Pakistani nationals linked to Harkat-ul-Mujahideen. It was flown to Amritsar, Lahore and Dubai before being forced to land in Kandahar, Afghanistan. The week-long hostage crisis ended on December 31 after the Indian government handed three jailed militants — including Masood Azhar, who went on to found Jaish-e-Mohammed — over to the Taliban, which then controlled most of Afghanistan, including Kandahar, in exchange for the release of the passengers and crew.

India did not wait for any explanation from Kathmandu. Indian Airlines was asked to suspend its flights to Kathmandu. The suspension lasted five months. No other international carriers stopped flying to Kathmandu during that time.

Following the visit of Chakra Prasad Bastola, the then foreign minister, to India on May 7, 2000, the two countries agreed to restore the suspended flights. Indian Airlines resumed its Kathmandu service on June 1.

The resumption, however, came with unprecedented security measures at TIA — passengers travelling to India on Indian Airlines flights were required to undergo a separate security screening on the airport ramp after clearing Nepal’s own security checks.

Multiple officials, diplomats and foreign ministers told Kantipur that Nepal has never made any formal effort or diplomatic correspondence to remove the arrangement.

Nothing comparable applies to any other international carrier at Tribhuvan Airport. Qatar Airways, Turkish Airlines and Cathay Pacific all fly out of Kathmandu under the Nepal government’s security regimes, and their passengers board the flights after Nepali screening alone. So do passengers on Nepal Airlines flights to New Delhi, Bengaluru, and Mumbai — the same routes, the same destination airports, with no additional search.

In international civil aviation, airport security is fundamentally anchored in sovereignty. Under the framework of the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO), the responsibility for screening passengers and securing airport facilities rests with the state in which the airport is located.

While states cooperate closely on aviation security — sharing intelligence, harmonising standards and responding to specific threats — the operational control of passenger screening is normally carried out by national authorities or agencies acting under their mandate.

ICAO’s global standards, particularly Annex 17 on aviation security, do not provide for routine passenger screening by foreign security personnel inside another state’s airport operational areas. Foreign involvement is generally limited to advisory roles, technical cooperation, or onboard security measures such as air marshals. Even in high-security aviation environments, the underlying principle is that the host state retains control over who conducts screening and how it is administered.

Kantipur could not identify another instance of a comparable standing arrangement at a foreign commercial airport.

“The International Civil Aviation Organisation sets out the arrangements required for aviation security, and under it various countries deploy such security officers — in plain terms, sky marshals,” says Bharat Dhakal, a former deputy director of the Civil Aviation Authority of Nepal. “In the case of Indian airline flights, India permits boarding only after conducting an additional security check in the apron area. Both governments need to rethink this.”

Deep Kumar Upadhyaya, Nepal’s former ambassador to India, says he was told that India raised the proposal during a foreign minister-level visit from Nepal, but it was rejected.

According to him, Nepal instead gave a verbal understanding allowing Indian authorities to conduct separate security screening. What exactly that understanding entailed, he says, deserves closer scrutiny.

“After the hijacking of the Indian aircraft, India questioned the security of our airport and levelled serious allegations against Nepal and suspended flights to Kathmandu, and bilateral relations went through a difficult period,” Upadhyaya said, recalling the events that followed the hijacking 26 years ago. “They kept insisting that our airport was unsafe and refused to resume flights. The Nepali side continued to reject those allegations.”

Upadhyaya said India’s anger after the hijacking was understandable, but that New Delhi used the incident to cast doubt on Nepal’s entire security system.

“In reality, that distrust reflected India’s intention to establish a permanent security presence at the airport,” he said. “Through continued negotiations and dialogue aimed at normalising relations after the hijacking, Nepal eventually allowed Indian authorities to conduct additional security screening for Indian flights as a temporary arrangement.”

The temporary arrangement was never revisited.



“Nepal never made an effective effort to remove it. That is unfortunate,” he said.

Dhakal believes a narrative was built out of a single hijacking — that Nepal’s airport was unsafe — and that it was not true.

“There is a great deal of difference between the security arrangements of two or three decades ago and those of today,” he said.

***

Former deputy prime minister Kamal Thapa, who has served as both foreign and home minister, said he was unable to establish whether a written agreement authorizing the arrangement exists.

“I had heard that given Nepal’s limitations at the time of the hijacking, the then government granted permission for Indian flights departing from Kathmandu to carry out a separate security check on passengers who had already cleared our airport security,” Thapa said.

“The understanding is that the Indian security checks were introduced with verbal consent at the level of Nepal’s prime minister and foreign minister, without being made public, and that this silence has continued at that level to this day,” a former foreign secretary told Kantipur , requesting anonymity because he was not authorized to discuss confidential deliberations.

Deviram Sharma, a former chief of the National Investigation Department, said Nepal saw India as using its objections to Nepal’s security measures to advance its own objectives.

Sharma said India pressed Nepal on airport security management, and that officials within the Nepal government worked to advance the Indian proposal. He said he found those efforts suspicious at the time, but declined to go into specifics.

“Around 2005-06, I attended the meeting at the CAAN office as the NID chief, along with chiefs of other security agencies, including the Nepal Army’s operations commander,” he told Kantipur in an interview. “Of the several agenda items, one was a proposal to allow Indian sky marshals, which also outlined matters such as baggage and hand-carried luggage screening, as well as the security screening of passengers on Indian aircraft.”

According to him, the proposal, however, was unanimously rejected, as everyone was of the view that Nepal must not compromise on airport security.

“After that, the matter did not move forward,” he said.

What surprises him, he said, is that no Nepali government has ever taken a diplomatic initiative with India to state that the proposal was inappropriate and should be withdrawn.

According to Narayan Kaji Shrestha, a former deputy prime minister as well as foreign and home minister, around 2008, a proposal had also reached the Council of Ministers, through the Ministry of Tourism, to allow Indian sky marshals as requested by India.

The Cabinet, however, adopted a policy of neither approving nor rejecting the proposal, and simply did not take a decision, he said.

Indian security personnel have conducted additional checks on passengers flying from Kathmandu to India since the IC814 hijacking in 1999. Post file photo

According to a Ministry of Tourism official, who spoke on condition of anonymity, after the Cabinet failed to make a decision, then Tourism Minister Hisila Yami issued a ministerial decision on January 21, 2009, citing the need to “strengthen airport security.”

The official said that although the decision did not explicitly mention “Indian sky marshals,” it effectively institutionalised the practice by allowing Indian personnel to conduct security screening of passengers bound for India on the ramp. The ministry now says it cannot locate that decision.

Yami, who served as tourism minister in 2008-09 during Pushpa Kamal Dahal-led Maoist government following the Constituent Assembly elections, acknowledged that she took a favourable view of India's request to allow security equipment to be stationed at TIA so that Indian authorities could conduct separate screening of passengers boarding Indian flights, and that she acted accordingly.

Yami, who is the wife of former prime minister Baburam Bhattarai, said she has often been criticised in the name of “nationalism,” with allegations that she had authorised the deployment of Indian sky marshals. Rejecting that claim, she insisted that the issue during her tenure was not about permitting Indian sky marshals but about installing X-ray equipment.

“The Indian side was already conducting an additional security check using large X-ray machines and other equipment,” Yami told Kantipur . “Transporting those machines to and from the airport for every flight had become cumbersome, so they requested permission to keep the equipment at the airport.”

Though some officials had questioned why equipment used by the Indian side should be kept at the Nepali airport and why India should be conducting security checks, Yami said she saw it as a practical matter.

“I felt that allowing the equipment to remain at the airport would not cause any harm. That was why the decision was made,” she said.

That same equipment that was too cumbersome to move for each flight has now remained at the country’s main international airport for 17 years.

Asked what the decision contained, whether the Home Ministry’s opinion was sought before it was taken, and what operational procedures followed, Jay Narayan Acharya, spokesperson for the Ministry of Tourism, said the ministry could not locate the relevant documents.

“We searched for the files but could not find them. You may want to check with the Civil Aviation Authority of Nepal,” he said.

Kantipur then requested a copy of the decision from Mukesh Dangol, director general of the Civil Aviation Authority of Nepal. A few days later, Dangol responded that the authority could not locate the decision either and suggested contacting the Ministry of Tourism.

Kantipur also asked the Home Ministry for the letter in which the tourism ministry had sought its opinion on the screening arrangement. An official at the ministry said it was not possible to respond immediately because many government records had been destroyed during the Gen Z protests, and efforts to recover and compile older documents were still ongoing.

As a result, neither the ministry that made the decision nor the agencies responsible for implementing it were able — or willing — to produce the documents governing the arrangement.

“India, which had suspended flights to Nepal for nearly five months, agreed to resume operations only after it was allowed to conduct its own security screening,” said a former joint secretary at the Home Ministry.

Former Home Secretary Govinda Prasad Kusum, in his 2021 book Prashasan bhitrako Prashasan , recounts the pressure he says he received from then Indian Ambassador to Nepal Rakesh Sood over airport security arrangements.

India has also sought permission for sky marshals on flights from Kathmandu, but Nepali authorities have repeatedly rejected or shelved the proposals. Post file photo

According to the book and officials serving at the Home Ministry at the time, Ambassador Sood telephoned Kusum in January 2009 to press Nepal to allow Indian sky marshals at TIA. Kusum also writes that he was told the matter was already being taken to the Cabinet for a decision.

An excerpt from the conversation, published in the chapter titled The Indian Ambassador and the Sky Marshal (p. 47), reads in translation from Nepali:

Sood: “Approval should be given for deploying sky marshals on Indian aircraft departing from Tribhuvan International Airport.”

Kusum: “Matters relating to sky marshals do not fall within the Home Ministry's jurisdiction. Since this concerns civil aviation, it falls under the Ministry of Tourism and Civil Aviation. The proposal should be processed there and then taken to the Cabinet.”

Sood: “India has permitted sky marshals on flights in many countries. What political impact would it have in Nepal if Nepal allowed sky marshals on Indian aircraft flying here?”

Kusum: “Indian officials are already allowed to conduct comprehensive security screening near Indian aircraft on the ramp. No passenger can board without passing through your security checkpoint. What more do you need?”

Kusum’s book also recounts another exchange with Ambassador Sood. According to the book, in the final week of January 2009, before the Cabinet met, Ambassador Sood again telephoned the then home secretary.

“The Ministry of Tourism and Civil Aviation has sent the proposal to the Cabinet to approve the deployment of sky marshals,” Sood told him.

“Best of luck, Excellency!” Kusum replied.

The Cabinet, however, never publicly announced any decision on the matter.

Former prime minister Bhattarai, who was in charge from 2011 to 2013, has himself undergone the additional screening. Recently, a photograph of him, when he was no longer prime minister, standing in line before boarding an Indian Airlines flight from Kathmandu drew public attention.

As prime minister, Bhattarai paid an official visit to India in October 2011. During the visit, he and his Indian counterpart, Manmohan Singh, issued a joint press statement .

According to a former Nepali foreign secretary familiar with the visit, removing the Indian security screening at TIA was not part of the formal agenda. Instead, when Nepal requested three additional international air routes from India, New Delhi sought to institutionalise the Indian security screening arrangement as a condition.

Point 11 of the statement reads: “The Nepalese side requested the Government of India to allow three additional inbound air routes from Janakpur, Bhairahawa and Nepalgunj in view of increased air traffic to and from Nepal and for facilitating international air service from the regional airports of Nepal cost-effectively. The Indian side proposed a meeting of the civil aviation authorities of Nepal and India to discuss and address various issues in this sector.”

The joint statement makes no reference to security screening.

According to the former secretary, the proposal also reflected India’s intention to extend its security screening arrangement beyond Tribhuvan International Airport to Nepal’s regional airports. The proposal never materialised.

But neither did the routes. Nepal and India resumed talks on the same three entry points this year, after more than a decade.

In an interview with Kantipur, Bhattarai said that during his visit to India he had discussed the hijacking and related issues in parts.

Former prime minister Baburam Bhattarai has himself undergone the additional screening and says airport security should be addressed through a broader framework of Nepal-India relations, rather than on a case-by-case basis.

“I had told [the Indian side] that we should resolve the issue in a holistic way; I had even asked them what their security concerns were,” Bhattarai said. “I had even told them that ‘you call Nepal a close neighbour yet you refuse to accept Nepal’s sovereignty.’ I have said publicly that issues such as airport and border security, including security screening by Indian personnel at the airport, should not be handled on a case-by-case basis.”

Bhattarai said those issues should instead be addressed as part of the broader framework of Nepal–India development, security cooperation, and bilateral relations. “I continue to stand firmly by that position,” he added.

***

Almost every major political party in Nepal has at one point risen to power by championing nationalism and sovereignty. Yet none has publicly sought a review of the airport security arrangement with India.

When the Maoists launched their armed insurgency, many of their 40 demands centred on India and what they described as Indian interference in Nepal. They even spoke of taking the fight to India. Yet after coming to power, they took no steps to review the airport security arrangement. Nor has the issue received meaningful attention under successive governments led by the Nepali Congress, CPN-UML or other coalition partners. Governments changed. But the arrangement didn’t.

At present, 30 airlines make international flights from TIA, including two from India — Air India and IndiGo. Only passengers on those airlines face the second screening.

After the hijacking incident, Nepal strengthened airport security management and also mobilized counter-terrorism mechanisms within its security agencies.

Despite major upgrades to airport security over the past 26 years, the additional Indian screening remains in place only for Air India and IndiGo passengers. Post file photo

Nepal has substantially expanded security at Tribhuvan over the past 26 years. At least 500 police personnel are now deployed, against about 100 in 2000. The airport has 30 X-ray machines, 20 walk-through metal detectors and 80 hand-held detectors. Immigration issues printed boarding passes with barcodes, and close to 500 CCTV cameras are installed.

By the standards Nepal’s own auditors apply, that expansion has not closed the gap — and the shortfall is what sustains India’s argument for keeping its own arrangement in place.

A high-level committee report published last year on Nepal’s aviation security found that the security arrangement at TIA remains fragmented, outdated, and lacking effective coordination among agencies responsible for safeguarding the facility. The report, which was overseen by former Supreme Court Justice Anil Kumar Sinha, said that although multiple security bodies operate at the airport, overlapping responsibilities and separate chains of command have created accountability gaps, weakening overall security management.

“Nepal continues to rely on traditional screening practices, including repeated passenger checks and manual frisking, while lacking modern detection technologies used at major international airports,” the report said. The committee also highlighted the limited deployment of specialised aviation security personnel, weak perimeter and landside security, and insufficient preparedness to respond to threats such as terrorism and sabotage.

It recommended the creation of a dedicated aviation security force, stronger oversight under a clearly defined authority, and reforms to align TIA’s security framework with international standards.

Earlier this summer, Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal visited New Delhi from June 5 to 7 this year, the first high-level engagement since Prime Minister Balendra Shah’s government took office.

On June 6, 2026, Khanal said he had held “extensive and productive discussions” with his Indian counterpart S Jaishankar and delegations from both sides. He said the talks covered trade and economic cooperation, connectivity, energy partnership, water resources management, shared security, border management, sports, and the promotion of people-to-people relations.

During the visit, he also met India’s National Security Advisor Ajit Doval. That meeting, according to Khanal, involved an “exchange of views on various aspects of Nepal-India shared security concerns, border management, and different dimensions of the strategic partnership between the two countries.”

Khanal did not say what those security concerns were. Neither the Nepali nor the Indian readout of the Jaishankar meeting mentioned security; both listed trade, investment, connectivity, energy and people-to-people ties. Asked whether the Kathmandu screening was raised in Delhi, Khanal confirmed it was. “There have been talks with Indian officials on all such matters, including airport security,” he told Kantipur. “Beyond that, nothing more can be said at present.”

Former deputy prime minister Kamal Thapa says efforts should be made to remove the arrangement, which was put in place 26 years ago under circumstances that no longer exist.

“Back when the aircraft was hijacked, the security situation at Tribhuvan International Airport was different. There may have been limitations in resources and technological capacity, and the hijackers took advantage of that,” Thapa told the Post. “But the continuation of the arrangement allowing Indian security personnel to conduct security checks on passengers travelling on Indian flights is inappropriate and undesirable for a sovereign nation.”

title: Nepal’s international standing enhanced through active participation in UN General Assembly - english.khabarhub.com

full_article:
KATHMANDU: Nepal’s image and standing on the international stage have been enhanced through its active participation in the 81st United Nations General Assembly and related programmes, according to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

Prime Minister Balendra Shah returned home on Saturday after participating in the General Assembly. Briefing the media at Tribhuvan International Airport about the visit, Acting Foreign Secretary Ganesh Prasad Dhakal said Nepal’s active participation in the UN General Assembly had helped enhance the country’s standing internationally.

Prime Minister Shah had departed for New York on Ashoj 6 to attend the high-level week of the 81st UN General Assembly, being held at the UN headquarters from September 22 to 28.

Shah addressed the General Debate on September 24. According to Dhakal, he highlighted the devastating Bhotekoshi flood of last month as a serious impact of the climate crisis and a warning to the world.

Shah drew the international community’s attention to the heavy loss of life and property caused by the disaster and its impact on infrastructure and livelihoods.

He also highlighted the effects of climate change on mountain ecosystems and said the melting of glaciers and permafrost was increasing the risks of disasters including avalanches, floods and landslides.

During his address, Shah proposed establishing a “Himalayan Climate Resilience Mechanism” for monitoring vulnerable glacial lakes, strengthening early warning systems and improving cross-border coordination during disasters.

Shah also called for world peace, saying, “May the world be able to follow the path shown by Buddha,” Dhakal said.

During the visit, Shah held a meeting with UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres. Guterres expressed deep condolences over the loss of life and property in the Bhotekoshi disaster and said the United Nations stood in solidarity with Nepal on climate issues.

Shah thanked Guterres for his goodwill toward Nepal and congratulated him on his successful tenure. He also noted that Nepal had suffered significant losses from the Bhotekoshi disaster and that the risk of glacial lake outburst floods remained high.

Shah also held a meeting with Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, during which the two sides discussed various issues of bilateral interest.

Meanwhile, Acting Foreign Secretary Dhakal said Foreign Minister Shishir Khanal has been participating in ministerial-level meetings held during the General Assembly involving the Least Developed Countries, Landlocked Developing Countries, Non-Aligned Movement, Group of 77 and China, among others.

Khanal has also been addressing other high-level discussions and side events organised by the United Nations and holding meetings with his counterparts from neighbouring and friendly countries as well as senior UN officials.

Rescued worker ready to help rebuild Nepal

BY ANUP Ojha / AFP, KIRTIPUR, Nepal

Add TT as Preferred Source



Rescued alive 10 days after catastrophic floods trapped him in a tunnel, Nepalese hydropower worker Kabir Maharjan is determined to help rebuild his country despite his own harrowing ordeal.

Traditional music and tearful relatives welcomed the 45-year-old when he returned home on Friday after spending weeks recovering at a hospital in Kathmandu.

“Life is precious. Hundreds of people have died but I survived,” the father of two said in an interview, his voice choked with emotion. “Perhaps I still have work to do for my society, for the country, and my home and family.”

Soldiers disembark a helicopter carrying Kabir Maharjan, a worker who was trapped inside a tunnel of the Trishuli-3A Hydropower Project, as they arrive at Chhauni Army Hospital in Kathmandu on Sept. 4 Photo: AFP

The Aug. 26 flood, triggered by a glacial mountain collapse near the China-Nepal border, killed at least 1,400 people, the majority in Nepal.

More than 5,000 people remain missing in Nepal after the tsunami-like waves swept away roads, bridges and settlements in the mountainous northern regions, and battered crucial hydropower projects.

displayDFP('ad-IR1', 'm');

Maharjan, who was among hundreds of workers employed at projects hit by the floods, was eventually airlifted from the worst-hit Rasuwa region.

His miraculous rescue on Sept. 4, alongside fellow worker Sanjay Sah, offered a rare moment of hope during the disaster.

As Nepal shifts from emergency response to reconstruction, he said he hopes to return to his profession.

“There is risk in everything, but still we have to win over it,” he said.

In Nepal, more than 800 hydropower project workers remain unaccounted for, the energy minister told parliament last week.

Rescue teams continue to comb through the ruins, and 47 bodies have been recovered from flood-hit project sites.

Maharjan said he survived by reaching an upper floor of the tunnel site and drinking water while waiting for help.

“Whenever I was awake, I would try to find a way out,” he said. Days later, he saw what appeared to be a light and heard voices. “I thought I imagined it. But I called out, and they answered.”

For Maharjan, the country’s long road to recovery mirrors his own — he is still recovering from wounds on his hand and leg.

He said the rebuilding efforts could provide spiritual sustenance.

“While we are alive we must be patient and do our work,” he said. “Work is our karma.”

The flooding dealt a major blow to Nepal’s hydropower generation system, which is central to the country’s development ambitions and export earnings.

The government estimates overall reconstruction could cost US$4.8 billion, with thousands of people displaced and key infrastructure damaged.

The disaster has renewed scrutiny of how roads, hydropower plants and trade corridors are built in Nepal’s challenging mountain terrain.

Nepalese Prime Minister Balendra Shah told the UN on Thursday that the flooding was “a warning to the world” about the growing dangers posed by climate change, urging greater international support to help Nepal adapt and rebuild.

Aid groups have warned that the humanitarian crisis is far from over.

“The floodwaters may have receded, but for thousands of people, the crisis is far from over,” David Fisher, head of delegation for the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies in Nepal, said on Friday. “It is urgent to take the next steps in the recovery process to keep people healthy and avoid a spiral into poverty.”

title: Why the U.S. Did Not Send a Search-and-Rescue Team to Nepal: Luke Ortega Explains (Interview) - nepyork
description: Why the U.S. Did Not Send a Search-and-Rescue Team to Nepal: Luke Ortega Explains (Interview)  nepyork
publisher.title: nepyork
full_article:
The United States has provided more than $36 million in assistance to Nepal following the devastating floods that struck the country on Aug. 26, with support ranging from immediate humanitarian aid and food assistance to permanent bridges, medical and sanitation supplies, disaster-recovery drones and forensic assistance to help locate and identify missing people. In an interview with NepYork Editor-in-Chief Kishor Panthi, Luke Ortega, currently serving as Deputy Spokesman for the U.S. Department of State, discussed the U.S. response, the decision not to deploy a search-and-rescue team, additional relief for communities affected by the disaster, climate justice and the status of about 70 Americans who remain unaccounted for.

Luke Ortega, deputy spokesman for the U.S. Department of State, speaks about the U.S. response to Nepal’s devastating floods. Photo by Rajan Kafle for NepYork.

KISHOR PANTHI: Could you tell me about the U.S. response to the disaster in Nepal following the devastating floods?

LUKE ORTEGA: Yes. Following those devastating floods in Nepal on August 26, the United States responded rapidly and efficiently, working with the authorities of Nepal in order to respond to that tragic disaster.

I want to give a sense of just what that response looked like coming from the United States. We have been able to provide more than $36 million in support to Nepal to respond to that flooding. And I want to explain what that means.

Get it all delivered straight to your inbox. Enter email address here... Click here to subscribe

We were able to initially provide about a million dollars in immediate humanitarian assistance to affected communities that were impacted by the flooding. We were also able to look toward the medium term and to be able to provide $3 million in food assistance that’s going to help to feed more than 10,000 families for three months.

We’ve provided as well approximately $10 million that we were able to announce just this week in order to produce custom-made bridges that are going to be permanent bridges made by U.S. companies to help replace some of that infrastructure that was damaged.

We’ve also increased an additional $8 million in terms of humanitarian supplies, sanitation, shelter, immediate health needs, and we’ve been able to provide $13 million in drone support to be able to support Nepal moving forward.

And I want to note as well a really key element of this, which is a million dollars that has come for forensic support for things like DNA kits. We take this very seriously in the United States. There are 70 Americans who remain unaccounted for following this flooding, and this forensic support, along with the participation of specialists from the Federal Bureau of Investigation, the FBI, will be able to help get families both in the United States and Nepal the answers they need.

KISHOR PANTHI: So many schools have been destroyed, and health posts have also been destroyed. Are you planning to send more relief to Nepal? Because this relief is focused on infrastructure development, such as bridges. Are you planning to send more relief for schools, health facilities and other infrastructure?

LUKE ORTEGA: Well, I want to emphasize that much of the humanitarian support that’s already been delivered is directed to try to help families that have been impacted by this flooding.

About $185,000 of the funding that went through Catholic Relief Services to Nepal was specifically aimed at helping children and families who had been impacted and creating resources for them in order to be safe in the immediate term there.

This is really an issue that has touched the hearts of Americans around the country. I’ve had the opportunity to talk to Americans around the country following this devastating flood, and it is something that has been really impactful for so many Americans who want to be able to help.

I want to emphasize that all of the U.S. support that is being delivered is done so in consultation, in conversation, with the authorities of Nepal, where they are able to identify the areas with need, and then the United States is acting and being proactive as well to be able to meet those needs.

“We really want to be able to identify concrete needs and then to be able to provide support to Nepal to be able to meet those needs,” Ortega said in an interview with NepYork Editor-in-Chief Kishor Panthi about the U.S. response to Nepal’s devastating floods. Photo by Rajan Kafle for NepYork.

KISHOR PANTHI: The United States couldn’t send a rescue team to Nepal. If the U.S. had been able to send a rescue team, do you think more lives could have been saved? Why didn’t you send a rescue team to Nepal?

LUKE ORTEGA: So, I want to again emphasize that the support that has come from the United States has come in consultation with the authorities in Nepal.

Initially, that’s true. The United States offered a search-and-rescue team, and at the time it was determined by the authorities in Nepal that that was not necessary for their needs there. We respected that, and we continued to provide really significant support in the immediate days following that terrible flooding.

I’ve mentioned some of the big-dollar things, but there’s a lot of very practical things that happen as well. The United States was able to deliver, for example, front-end loaders. If you think of sort of small bulldozers to help clear roads and move away some of that mud and debris, we were able to provide, for example, solar power generators to provide reliable electricity to communities that were impacted by the flooding.

And it was wonderful to see the whole embassy community, our embassy in Kathmandu, as well as our partners within the Nepali community, coming together to be able to provide three truckloads of support to impacted communities that they were able to locally provide to them as well.

KISHOR PANTHI: Does the United States view the recent disaster in Nepal as a global warning, as Nepal’s Prime Minister Shah framed it?

LUKE ORTEGA: Our priority is to be able to respond to disasters rapidly, to be able to respond to them effectively, and that’s something that I think we’ve been able to demonstrate in the case of the flooding in Nepal.

We’ve seen that as well with the Ebola outbreak in Africa, as well as with significant earthquakes in Colombia and Venezuela. The United States has been able to send, within hours after these terrible events, support directly, and that has to do with the way that we have worked to modernize, to streamline and to improve our ability to respond to disasters by really centralizing all of the actors involved in this.

Get them all around the same game table to be able to identify needs and respond rapidly to them, and we’re proud to be able to support Nepal in this moment.

KISHOR PANTHI: The Nepali prime minister’s speech was focused on climate change and climate justice yesterday. About 70% of his speech was focused on climate justice and climate change. Nepal is seeking climate justice. Will the United States help Nepal in its efforts to obtain climate justice?

LUKE ORTEGA: We continue to engage with Nepal authorities at the highest levels. Secretary of State Marco Rubio has spoken to leaders in Nepal. Our diplomats there at our embassy have been able to speak to the prime minister and to those around him.

We remain in constant contact there, and we really want to be able to identify concrete needs and then to be able to provide support to Nepal to be able to meet those needs.

KISHOR PANTHI: Do you have any message for the families of Americans who are unaccounted for? There are around 70 Americans who are unaccounted for.

LUKE ORTEGA: That’s right. I want to make sure that these numbers are clear. We are aware of 70 Americans who are unaccounted for. We’re also aware of 18 Americans who’ve been able to make it to safety. And at this point, we’re unable to confirm American deaths as a result of this flooding.

But as I mentioned, this is part of the reason why at the State Department, we are working in order to provide that forensic support to get those answers. We understand that at this point they may be hard answers, but they are important answers for families to get.

We are working to be in proactive contact with Americans who have been impacted, and I want to encourage any Americans who need to be in contact with the State Department to reach out to us at travel.state.gov to be able to get into contact with us and to get into contact with the office that works with American citizens impacted by this unfortunate event.

KISHOR PANTHI: The Nepali community in the United States is seeking Temporary Protected Status, or TPS, following the disaster in Nepal. The United States designated TPS for Nepal after the 2015 earthquake as well. So, right now, they are seeking TPS again. I know the Department of Homeland Security will make the decision on this, but I think it will also consider a report from the U.S. Department of State. Do you have any comment on this?

LUKE ORTEGA: I have nothing to announce about this particular area. As you mentioned, this will fundamentally be a decision for the Department of Homeland Security.

As I mentioned, I have had the opportunity to engage with Americans around the country, including in cities with significant populations of people from Nepal. We understand the pain that so many people are feeling, and that’s why the United States has mobilized this support to be fast and effective, to provide the assistance that we can.

title: B.C. family still looking for answers 1 month after deadly Nepal flood - CBC
description: B.C. family still looking for answers 1 month after deadly Nepal flood  CBC
publisher.title: CBC
full_article:
One month after a deadly flooding event in Nepal, a B.C. family is among several Canadians still waiting for answers.

Over 1,400 bodies have been recovered and over 5,600 people remain missing — the Canadian Press reports — a month after a catastrophic flash flood struck the Himalayan border between Nepal and Tibet on Aug. 26.

Global Affairs Canada said on Saturday that 29 Canadians and permanent residents remain missing.

Coquitlam, B.C., couple Sumit and Shubakshi Rawla are among them, according to family.

"We are still clueless," said Shubakshi’s cousin Vikram Khosla.

The couple lived with their two daughters — one a teenager and one in her early 20s, he said.

"We are helpless, we can’t do anything," said Khosla.

2 trapped workers rescued from hydropower tunnel 9 days after Nepal floods

He said the couple and their two daughters had been in India visiting family at the time, when Sumit and Shubakshi took a trip to the Himalayas for a trek to Kailash Mansarovar in Tibet, a sacred site for Hindus, Buddhists and others.

The couple spoke with a family member about an hour before the flood struck, but nobody has heard from them since then, said Khosla.

He said the daughters are back in Canada and various family members are taking turns caring for them.

WATCH | Why the Nepal flood was almost impossible to predict: Why you can’t predict a disaster like Nepal’s flood | About That September 3 | Duration 2:58 A collapsed glacier in Nepal caused catastrophic flooding that killed more than a thousand people, while thousands more are still missing. Andrew Chang breaks down what accelerated the flood to such a violent degree and how factors like the scale of the Himalayan mountains and the region's climate make prediction and monitoring so challenging. (Photo credits: The Canadian Press, Reuters, Adobe Stock and Getty Images)

The federal government says Canadian officials continue to work with authorities in Nepal and China to support efforts to locate the missing Canadians and provide assistance to affected families.

"Due to privacy considerations, no further information can be provided, and we cannot comment on what is being discussed with families," said the statement.

Global Affairs Canada would not specify how many of the missing Canadians are from B.C., but CBC News has spoken with the family of another missing couple from Port Moody — Dhaval and Megha Shah .

Sumit and Shubakshi Rawla, pictured with loved ones, are among 29 Canadians still missing since the flash flood, according to family members. (Submitted by Vikram Khosla)

Despite no news on his cousin, Khosla says the family holds onto hope that they can be found.

"Everyone keeps praying every single day, hoping that maybe they are injured, maybe they are somewhere stuck and maybe we will get to hear something about them," he said.

Khosla described the couple as "beautiful souls." He said the couple took care of others and were part of a very happy family.

"It’s hard to believe that something like that happened to them," he said. "I don’t know why they had to be there at that time."

title: U.S. Says It Seeks to Expand Economic Ties With Nepal, Not Force Geopolitical Choices - nepyork

publisher.title: nepyork
full_article:
NEW YORK — The United States does not intend to ask Nepal to choose between Washington, Beijing and New Delhi. Instead, it wants to offer Kathmandu economic and commercial alternatives, a senior State Department official told NepYork.

“Similar to Bangladesh, where I don’t think we’re going to any country — and you’ll hear the Secretary talk about this — and say you have to choose,” the official said when asked how the United States views Nepal’s sovereignty as the Himalayan nation balances its relations with India and China.

“But what we want to do is we want to provide alternatives,” the official said. “We want to provide — for Nepal in particular, we’ve been very interested in increasing our commercial engagement.”

The official said the United States sees investment and business ties as a key area for strengthening the bilateral relationship.

“So for the first time ever this year, Nepal — I think they amended their law last year about outbound investment,” the official said. “We had the first Nepali delegation come to SelectUSA, the event that the Department of Commerce hosts.”

U.S. Chargé d’Affaires, a.i. Megan Bouldin meets with Acting Prime Minister and Finance Minister Dr. Swarnim Wagle this week to discuss Nepal’s flood recovery and long-term reconstruction.

“This is a first step in how we do investments into Nepal,” the official said. “We want to make a better business environment and business climate. We want our companies there, and we want Nepali companies to be in the U.S.”

Asked about Nepal’s efforts to balance its relations with its two larger neighbors, the official acknowledged the country’s difficult geopolitical position.

“And so when we talk about balancing, we understand Nepal — I mean, you look at the map,” the official said. “They’re in a very — they’re in a tough spot in the world.”

The official said Nepal maintains a strong relationship with India and that Washington wants Nepal to have greater opportunities to deepen ties with the United States and other Western countries.

“They have a good relationship with India, and we want — we want to be able to provide that opportunity for them to also look to the West and have better relations with us,” the official said. “And that’s what we’re building towards.”
